issues.legal_issue: A transferee who acquires an interest in property during a suit may apply to set aside an ex parte decree entered against the transferor, even if the transferee was not brought on record.
material_facts: During the suit over immovable property, a purchaser acquired the property from the defendants.
The suit was later decreed ex parte against the defendants.
The purchaser had not been brought on record and applied to set aside the decree, also seeking to be brought on record.
The purchaser was a transferee pendente lite and would be bound by the decree and exposed to its execution.
issues.conclusion: The transferee was entitled to apply under Order 9 Rule 13 to set aside the ex parte decree against the transferor, notwithstanding that the transferee had not been brought on record under Order 22 Rule 10.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act embodies the doctrine of lis pendens: a transfer during litigation does not defeat the successful party’s rights, and the transferee is bound by the decree. Order 22 Rule 10 gives the court discretion to bring a person on record after a devolution of interest; doing so is not a right, and a transferee remains bound by the decree even if not joined. Under Section 146 CPC, a person claiming under another may take a proceeding or make an application that the other could have taken or made. Read liberally, Section 146 permits a lis pendens transferee who stands in the defendant’s shoes to apply under Order 9 Rule 13. The Court relied on Smt. Saila Bala Dassi v. Sm. Nirmala Sundari Dassi, Jugalkishore Saraf v. M/s. Raw Cotton Co. Ltd., and Sardar Govindrao Mahadik v. Devi Sahai; it distinguished Surjit Singh v. Harbans Singh, where impleadment was refused in the circumstances of a transfer made in defiance of an injunction.

rule.if: ex_parte_set_aside_application and interest_transferred_during_suit and decree_entered_against_transferor and transferee_not_brought_on_record

predicates.ex_parte_set_aside_application: A person applies to set aside an ex parte decree.
predicates.interest_transferred_during_suit: A person acquires an interest in the subject property from a litigant while the suit is pending.
predicates.decree_entered_against_transferor: The ex parte decree is entered against the person who transferred the interest.
predicates.transferee_not_brought_on_record: The person who acquired the interest was not brought on record in the suit.

issues.definition: When a person applies to set aside an ex parte decree entered against a transferor after acquiring an interest during the suit, the person may make that application even if not brought on record.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that sufficient cause existed to set aside an ex parte decree and condone delay may be upheld when it is a well-reasoned finding of fact.
material_facts: The purchaser said that the ex parte decree was not known to the purchaser, explaining the delay in applying.
The trial court condoned the delay and found sufficient cause to set aside the decree.
The Supreme Court considered that finding factual and well reasoned.
issues.conclusion: The finding in favour of the purchaser on sufficient cause and condonation of delay was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Order 9 Rule 13 CPC requires sufficient cause for setting aside an ex parte decree, and Section 5 of the Limitation Act governs condonation of delay. The Court treated whether sufficient cause existed on these facts as a factual determination and found the trial court’s reasoned finding sustainable.

predicates.ex_parte_set_aside_application: A person applies to set aside an ex parte decree after time has passed.
predicates.applicant_unaware_of_decree: The applicant did not know that the ex parte decree had been entered.
predicates.lower_court_found_sufficient_cause: The lower court found sufficient cause for setting aside the decree and excusing the delay.

issues.definition: When an applicant unaware of an ex parte decree seeks to set it aside and the lower court finds sufficient cause, that finding and the resulting condonation are upheld.
